content.text: An averaged F1 score isn't a summary of every class. Each average decides how much each class counts: micro F1 equals accuracy in single-label multiclass, and weighted F1 follows the biggest class. Here, weighted F1 preferred a ticket router that caught 15 of 38 security tickets over one that caught 35. Read the per-class scores first, then choose the average that matches what you care about.

A support team routes incoming tickets with a classifier: billing, technical, account, refunds and security. The model card says weighted F1 0.924. A candidate trained with class weights scores 0.918, so the team keeps the original. Two weeks later the security lead asks why account-takeover reports sit in the account queue for days. On the test set the original model sent 15 of the 38 security tickets there and routed only 15 correctly. The rejected candidate routed 35. No number on the model card could have shown it.
The common misconception
Many developers read a multiclass F1 score as a summary of every class: if the overall number is high, each class must be in decent shape. It's an easy belief to hold:

items.text: F1 is the metric you switch to when accuracy misleads, so it feels like the fair one by default.
refuses multiclass targets until you choose an
, so whichever one you pick looks like the official answer.
Weighted averaging sounds like the careful choice: the documentation says it accounts for label imbalance.

content.text: The half-truth: every average is built from per-class scores, so each class is in there somewhere. But each average also decides how much each class counts, and for a rare class the answer can be "almost nothing".
What actually happens
For a multiclass problem, scikit-learn computes precision, recall and
F1
once per class, treating that class as positive and all the others as negative. Then the
average
parameter collapses those per-class scores into one number. The three averages answer three different questions.
Micro F1 is accuracy under another name
average="micro"

pools the true positives, false positives and false negatives of all classes before dividing. In single-label multiclass, every wrong prediction is a false positive for the class it chose and a false negative for the class it missed, so the totals match. The scikit-learn guide states the result: with all labels included, micro precision, recall and F1 are all identical to accuracy.
classification_report
doesn't even print a micro average in that case, because it would repeat accuracy. Micro F1 is a fine metric; it just isn't a different one from the accuracy you were trying to get away from.
Weighted F1 follows the biggest class
average="weighted"

averages the per-class scores weighted by support, the number of true examples of each class. In the test set below, billing has 683 of 1,250 tickets and security has 38, so billing carries a weight of 0.55 and security 0.03. The documentation adds a quirk: a weighted F1 can even fall outside the range between the weighted precision and recall.
Macro F1 gives every class one vote
average="macro"
is the plain mean of the per-class scores. A rare class counts as much as the biggest one, which is why the scikit-learn guide suggests
macro averaging
when infrequent classes still matter. Here are both candidates, judged first by the two averages that count tickets, then class by class.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# five ticket queues: billing, technical, account, refunds, security
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=5000, n_features=10, n_informative=6,
                           n_classes=5, n_clusters_per_class=1, class_sep=1.2,
                           weights=[0.55, 0.25, 0.1, 0.07], random_state=3)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
for cw in [None, "balanced"]:
    pred = LogisticRegression(class_weight=cw).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)
    micro = f1_score(y_te, pred, average="micro")
    weighted = f1_score(y_te, pred, average="weighted")
    print(f"class_weight={cw}: micro {micro:.3f}, weighted {weighted:.3f}")
# class_weight=None: micro 0.927, weighted 0.924
# class_weight=balanced: micro 0.914, weighted 0.918

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, recall_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# five ticket queues: billing, technical, account, refunds, security
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=5000, n_features=10, n_informative=6,
                           n_classes=5, n_clusters_per_class=1, class_sep=1.2,
                           weights=[0.55, 0.25, 0.1, 0.07], random_state=3)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
for cw in [None, "balanced"]:
    pred = LogisticRegression(class_weight=cw).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)
    macro = f1_score(y_te, pred, average="macro")
    print(f"class_weight={cw}: macro F1 {macro:.3f}")
    print("  recall per queue", recall_score(y_te, pred, average=None).round(2))
# class_weight=None: macro F1 0.815
#   recall per queue [0.98 0.95 0.82 0.82 0.39]
# class_weight=balanced: macro F1 0.832
#   recall per queue [0.95 0.93 0.75 0.83 0.92]

content.text: By micro and weighted F1 the two models are nearly tied, and both numbers prefer the original: 0.927 against 0.914, 0.924 against 0.918. The micro scores are exactly the two models' accuracies. Class by class, the story changes: the original finds 39% of security tickets, the class-weighted model 92%, while billing recall slips from 0.98 to 0.95. Macro F1 sees that trade and prefers the candidate, 0.832 against 0.815.

Weighted F1 moved the other way for a simple reason. Billing's F1 fell by 0.013 with a weight of 0.55, which costs 0.007. Security's F1 rose from 0.500 to 0.625 with a weight of 0.03, which adds 0.004. With a small loss on account tickets too, the total drops by 0.006. Weighted F1 did what it's built to do: count tickets, not queues.
Macro F1 is a policy too

Macro isn't automatically right. The scikit-learn guide warns that treating all classes as equally important is often untrue, and macro averaging then over-emphasizes the typically low score of a rare class. Rare classes are also noisy: with 38 security tickets, one ticket moves security recall by 2.6 points. And "macro F1" has two definitions in the literature: scikit-learn averages the per-class F1 scores, while others take the F1 of the averaged precision and recall. Opitz and Burst show the two can rank classifiers differently; for the original model here they give 0.815 and 0.822. When you compare with a paper, check which one it used.

is macro-averaged recall: here it moves from 0.792 to 0.876, the change that accuracy hid. For a guardrail, track the worst class too, the minimum of
recall_score(..., average=None)
, so a model can't improve on average while one queue collapses.

blocks.title: Classes can drop out of the average

content.text: By default the labels come from
y_true
and
y_pred
, so a class missing from both, which happens in small folds, is silently left out of the macro average. Pass
labels=
with the full class list so every fold averages over the same classes. A class the model never predicts has an undefined precision: scikit-learn sets it to 0 and raises
UndefinedMetricWarning
, and
zero_division
changes that value. Choose it on purpose.
How to apply it in your project
Run
classification_report
on every evaluation: precision, recall, F1 and support for each class, plus accuracy and the macro and weighted averages.

items.title: Choose the average from the question

content.text: If every example matters equally, accuracy or weighted F1 fit. If every class matters, use macro. Write the choice and the reason in the model card.
Give classes like security a minimum recall, and fail any model below it, whatever its average.
Pass
labels=
explicitly, stratify your folds, and set
zero_division
deliberately, so averages compare across folds and models.
A
confusion matrix
shows that the missing security tickets landed in the account queue, which tells you what to fix next.
Key takeaways

items.text: Every average is a weighting policy: micro and weighted count examples, macro counts classes.
In single-label multiclass, micro F1 is exactly accuracy.
Weighted F1 preferred the model that missed 23 of 38 security tickets; per-class recall showed 0.39 against 0.92.
Report per-class scores with support, choose the average on purpose, and guard critical classes with a floor.
